newsitem.title: CHINA: Red Cross says to step up North Korea food relief.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross says to step up North Korea food relief.

text.p: The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies will expand food aid to North Korea to help stave off famine as the hungry country waits for its next harvest, a Red Cross official said on Saturday.

A recent increase in donations to the hermit nation through the Red Cross meant the agency could boost food aid to more than 700,000 people from 139,000 now, said Geoffery Dennis, director of the British Red Cross international department.

"People are really suffering," Dennis said in Beijing after a trip to the Stalinist country, which international aid workers say is facing the spectre of famine after several years of economic collapse and natural disasters.
"Grain warehouses are now empty or almost empty," Dennis said in an interview. "It will be a very critical situation up to the next harvest."

A Red Cross team on a two-week tour of North Korean villages and cities had found that 16.6 percent of the several hundred children under the age of six they surveyed were suffering from malnutrition, Dennis said.
"People are eating grassroots," he said. "People are eating bark, they're grinding it up and mixing it with other food."

North Korea would have a food shortage of about two million tonnes of grain in 1997, and many residents were living on a mere 100-150 grammes (3.5-5.3 ounces) of grain a day -- far below the subsistence level, Dennis said.

Cruel floods over the past two years have destroyed much of North Korea's grain harvests, further putting the squeeze on Pyongyang, already badly hit by the 1991 collapse of aid from communist ally the Soviet Union.
"Five million tonnes is the absolute maximum harvest for the country this year. The total need will be 7.4 million tonnes," Dennis said.
"I don't think they'll reach it," he said, adding that farm machinery was broken down and great swathes of cropland still buried under sand left by the floods.
North Korea's 23 million people had managed to ward off famine because most rural families were able to grow small amounts of food on tiny vegetable plots, he said.
"The cities are worse off than the countryside because people there can't grow their own food," he said. "Most people work in factories, which are running at about 30-40 percent capacity now."

The new Red Cross operation would be expanded to 19 counties and cities from the current 15 and would run from July 1 to November, when October harvest results could be confirmed, he said. Some 50,000 tonnes of food would be distributed.
The Red Cross would also pump $2.25 million into programmes to provide basic drugs and medical equipment to hospitals and health clinics in the target areas, he said.
"Hospitals... have virtually no drugs... except local herb-based medicines," he said, adding that hospitals were running at about 10 percent of capacity.
The South Korean Red Cross, which last week hammered out an accord with the North to deliver 50,000 tonnes of grain aid, had made substantial donations to the International Federation, Dennis said.

Capitalist Seoul and communist Pyongyang have been technically at war since their 1950-53 war ended only in a truce, and decades of mutual mistrust have made such assistance a delicate diplomatic affair.
